title: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
summary: How exact, tiled attention maps onto GPUs: the FlashAttention-2 loop, its Hopper redesign (warp specialization, ping-pong, FP8) and Blackwell redesign (software exp, TMEM, 2-CTA), and how to measure it.
outcomes: Compute online softmax block by block, including the rescaling step, and explain why the result is exact
Trace the tiled FlashAttention-2 forward and backward loops, including causal tile skipping and the D = rowsum(dO * O) step
Compute attention FLOPs, HBM bytes and exp-to-matmul time ratios, and utilization from reported TFLOPs/s
Explain FlashAttention-3's producer/consumer warp specialization, ping-pong and intra-warpgroup pipelining
Explain how block quantization and incoherent processing make FP8 attention more accurate
Explain FlashAttention-4's response to Blackwell: software exp2, conditional rescaling, TMEM and 2-CTA MMA

lessons.title: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time

blocks.md:
Attention for one head computes $S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d}$, where $d$ is the head dimension (the length of each query and key vector), takes a row-wise softmax to get $P$, then $O = PV$. With sequence length $N$, $S$ and $P$ are $N \times N$. The naive kernel writes them to HBM (the GPU's off-chip DRAM) and reads them back, and at $N = 8192$ that is 128 MiB per head per matrix in FP16: $8192^2 = 67{,}108{,}864$ entries at 2 bytes each is $2^{27}$ bytes, and a mebibyte is $2^{20}$ bytes.

The obstacle to keeping everything on chip is the softmax: each output needs the max and the sum over **all** $N$ scores in its row, but the chip's fast memory only holds a few blocks of keys at a time. The max is there for safety: kernels compute $e^{s_i - \max} / \sum_j e^{s_j - \max}$, which equals plain softmax because the factor $e^{-\max}$ cancels top and bottom, and it keeps every exponential at or below 1 so nothing overflows FP16, whose largest value is 65504.

**Online softmax** removes that obstacle. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) processes the keys and values in blocks and keeps three running quantities per query row: the max seen so far $m$, the sum of exponentials $l = \sum e^{s - m}$ (each taken relative to $m$), and an unnormalized output $O$. When a new block raises the max, the old $l$ and $O$ are multiplied by a **correction factor** $e^{m_{old} - m_{new}}$ so everything stays relative to the same max. The papers call the number of query rows in a tile $B_r$ (r for the rows of $S$) and the number of keys in a block $B_c$ (c for its columns); the example below has $B_r = 1$ and $B_c = 2$.

blocks.tex: m_j = \max(m_{j-1}, \mathrm{rowmax}(S_j)),\quad l_j = e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, l_{j-1} + \mathrm{rowsum}(e^{S_j - m_j}),\quad O_j = e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_j} V_j
blocks.caption: Block $j$ update, as in the FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-4 papers. In words: the new max is the larger of the old max and this block's max; old $l$ and $O$ shrink by $e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}$, then this block's exponentials are added to $l$ and, times its values, to $O$. At the end, output $= O / l$.

blocks.md: Here is a tiny example you can check by hand: one query, 6 keys with scores already scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$, a scalar value per key, and blocks of 2 keys. All numbers below were computed with a script.

blocks.title: One query row, 6 keys, processed in 3 blocks of 2

scenes.caption: Start: the running max $m$ is $-\infty$, the running sum $l$ is 0 and the unnormalized output $O$ is 0. Only the 6 scores and 6 values exist; the kernel will see them 2 at a time.

Block 2 brings a 5, so $m$ jumps from 3 to 5. Old weights shrink by $e^{3-5} = 0.1353$ (0.1353 becomes 0.0183, 1 becomes 0.1353), and $l$ and $O$ shrink by the same factor before the new terms are added.
Block 3 has max 4, below 5, so the correction factor is $e^{0} = 1$ and nothing old changes. New weights 0.0111 and 0.3679 give $l = 1.5824$ and $O = 67.012$.
Final step: divide once, $O/l = 67.012 / 1.5824 = 42.347$. A full softmax over all 6 scores gives exactly the same 42.347: online softmax is exact, not an approximation.

blocks.prompt: Before block 3 the running max is 5. Block 3's scores are 0.5 and 4. What correction factor is applied to the old $l$ and $O$?
blocks.reveal: **1.** The new max is $\max(5, 4) = 5$, unchanged, so the factor is $e^{5-5} = 1$ and the old state is untouched. Rescaling only matters when the max actually grows. Keep this in mind: FlashAttention-4 turns it into an optimization that skips most rescales.

blocks.title: The same loop as code (one query row, scalar values)
blocks.code:
m, l, O = -inf, 0.0, 0.0
for S_blk, V_blk in blocks:
    m_new = max(m, max(S_blk))
    c = exp(m - m_new)          # correction factor
    p = [exp(s - m_new) for s in S_blk]
    l = c * l + sum(p)
    O = c * O + dot(p, V_blk)
    m = m_new
out = O / l                     # one division at the end
lse = m + log(l)                # saved for the backward pass

scenes.caption: Three numbers per query row are all the state the kernel keeps. In the real kernel each is a vector over the $B_r$ rows of a query tile.
Second block: the max rises from 3 to 5, so the correction factor is $e^{3-5} = 0.1353$.
Old $l$ and $O$ are rescaled, then the block's own contribution (computed against the new max) is added.

After the last block: one division gives the output, and the log-sum-exp $L = m + \log l$ is saved: since $l = \sum e^{s-m}$, $L$ is the log of $\sum e^{s}$ over the whole row, so the backward pass can rebuild $P = e^{S - L}$ without storing it.

blocks.md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

A few GPU terms used from here on (the GPU and inference basics course covers them in full). A GPU is built from **streaming multiprocessors (SMs)**, independent compute units (132 on an H100). Each SM has its own registers, a small fast scratchpad called **shared memory** (SMEM), and **tensor cores**, units that multiply small matrix tiles in hardware. A **kernel** (a function launched on the GPU) runs as a grid of **thread blocks**; each block runs on one SM and uses that SM's shared memory, and its threads execute in **warps**, groups of 32 threads that issue the same instruction together.

FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2023) kept this math and changed the bookkeeping: it keeps $O$ unnormalized and divides by $l$ once at the end (fewer non-matmul operations), makes the outer loop run over query blocks so different thread blocks can work on different query blocks of the same head, and splits each query block across warps instead of splitting the keys (the "split-K" scheme) so warps no longer exchange partial results through shared memory. The next lesson builds that kernel tile by tile.

blocks.question: A kernel rescales $O$ by $e^{m_{old}-m_{new}}$ when the max grows but forgets to rescale $l$. What happens to the output in the example above?
options: Nothing, because $l$ only matters for the first block
The output becomes too large, because $l$ is too small
The output becomes too small, because $l$ keeps old terms at their larger, unscaled size
The kernel overflows, because $l$ grows without bound
blocks.explain: Without the factor, block 1's contribution stays at 1.1353 instead of 0.1536 in $l$, so the denominator is too big while $O$ is correct. Dividing gives a value biased toward zero. The bug only shows up when a later block raises the max, which is why it can survive simple tests.

blocks.question: Besides the output tile $O_i$, what does the FlashAttention forward kernel write to HBM for each query row, and why?
options: The full row of $P$, so the backward pass can reuse it
The log-sum-exp $L = m + \log l$, so the backward pass can recompute $P$ from $Q$ and $K$ without storing it
Nothing else; the backward pass recomputes $m$ and $l$ from scratch with a separate reduction
The running max $m$ only, since $l$ can be derived from $O$
blocks.explain: Algorithm 1 in the FlashAttention-3 paper ends by writing $O_i$ and $L_i = m_i + \log(\ell_i)$. One number per row is enough to recompute $P = \exp(S - L)$ block by block in the backward pass, which is how FlashAttention avoids storing the $N \times N$ matrix.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-2 kernel tile by tile: forward, backward, parallelism

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 ran online softmax for one query row. The real kernel does the same for a whole **tile** of query rows at once. It cuts $Q$ into $T_r = \lceil N/B_r \rceil$ tiles $Q_i$ of size $B_r \times d$, and $K$ and $V$ into $T_c = \lceil N/B_c \rceil$ tiles $K_j$, $V_j$ of size $B_c \times d$. The grid has one thread block per (batch, head, query tile). Each thread block loads its $Q_i$ once, then loops over $j$: load $K_j$ and $V_j$, compute the $B_r \times B_c$ score tile $S_{ij} = Q_i K_j^\top$ on the tensor cores, update $m$ and $l$ (now vectors, one entry per row) and the unnormalized $O_i$. At the end it divides $O_i$ by $l$ and writes $O_i$ and $L_i = m + \log l$ to HBM, once.

The tiny example below has $N = 6$ tokens, head dimension $d = 4$ and $B_r = B_c = 2$, so the $6 \times 6$ score matrix is a $3 \times 3$ grid of tiles. All numbers come from the script further down (random inputs, seed 0).

blocks.title: The 6 x 6 score matrix as a 3 x 3 grid of 2 x 2 tiles

scenes.caption: The full $S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d}$. The kernel never holds all of it; it sees one $2 \times 2$ tile at a time. Follow the thread block for query tile 2 (rows q4 and q5).
Step 1: load $K_0, V_0$ and compute tile $S_{2,0}$. Row maxes so far: $-0.23$ for q4 and $0.48$ for q5.
Step 2: tile $S_{2,1}$ brings 1.14 into row q4, so q4's max rises and its old $l$ and $O$ are scaled by 0.255. Row q5's max stays 0.48, factor 1.
Step 3: tile $S_{2,2}$ raises both maxes, to 1.30 and 0.80. Then the thread block divides by $l$ and writes 2 rows of $O$ and 2 values of $L$. Other thread blocks did q0 to q3 in parallel.

Causal masking hides every score whose key comes after the query. Tiles $S_{0,1}$, $S_{0,2}$ and $S_{1,2}$ are fully masked, so they are never loaded; diagonal tiles are loaded and masked inside. 6 of 9 tiles are visited.

blocks.title: On-chip state of the thread block for query tile 2

scenes.caption: Start: $Q_2$ is loaded into shared memory once and stays for the whole loop. $m$ is $-\infty$ and $l$ is 0 for both rows; the $2 \times 4$ accumulator $O_2$ is zero in registers.
Tile 0: the first factor is $e^{-\infty} = 0$ (there is no old state). $m = (-0.23, 0.48)$, $l = (1.513, 1.679)$.
Tile 1 overwrites the $K$ and $V$ slots. Row q4's max jumps to 1.14, so its old $l$ and $O$ shrink by 0.255 before the new terms are added; row q5 is unchanged (factor 1).
Tile 2 raises both maxes (factors 0.851 and 0.722). $l = (3.108, 3.595)$.
One division per row, then the only HBM writes: two rows of $O$ and $L = m + \log l = (2.433, 2.085)$, which equals the log of each row's full $\sum_k e^{s_k}$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, d, Br, Bc = 6, 4, 2, 2
Q, K, V = (rng.standard_normal((N, d)) for _ in range(3))
scale = 1 / np.sqrt(d)

def flash_fwd(causal=False):
    O, L, seen = np.zeros((N, d)), np.zeros(N), []
    for i in range(0, N, Br):            # one thread block per query tile
        m, l = np.full(Br, -np.inf), np.zeros(Br)
        acc = np.zeros((Br, d))          # unnormalized O_i, on chip
        for j in range(0, N, Bc):
            if causal and j > i + Br - 1:
                break                    # tile entirely above diagonal
            seen.append((i // Br, j // Bc))
            S = Q[i:i+Br] @ K[j:j+Bc].T * scale
            if causal:
                r = np.arange(i, i + Br)[:, None]
                c = np.arange(j, j + Bc)[None, :]
                S = np.where(c > r, -np.inf, S)
            m_new = np.maximum(m, S.max(1))
            P = np.exp(S - m_new[:, None])
            corr = np.exp(m - m_new)
            l = corr * l + P.sum(1)
            acc = corr[:, None] * acc + P @ V[j:j+Bc]
            m = m_new
        O[i:i+Br] = acc / l[:, None]
        L[i:i+Br] = m + np.log(l)        # log-sum-exp for backward
    return O, L, seen

def naive(causal=False):
    S = Q @ K.T * scale
    if causal:
        S = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((N, N)), 1) > 0, -np.inf, S)
    P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return (P / P.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ V

for causal in (False, True):
    O, L, seen = flash_fwd(causal)
    print(causal, np.allclose(O, naive(causal)), len(seen), seen)
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU with NumPy. Output: `False True 9 [...]` then `True True 6 [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), (2, 1), (2, 2)]`. Both match naive softmax attention, and the causal run visits 6 of the 9 tiles.

blocks.md:
**What sits where.** Real tiles are large. At $d = 128$ with $B_r = B_c = 128$ in BF16 (2 bytes per element), $Q_i$, $K_j$ and $V_j$ are $128 \times 128 \times 2$ bytes = 32 KiB each: 96 KiB of shared memory. The score tile $S_{ij}$ and the accumulator $O_i$ stay in FP32 registers, $128 \times 128 \times 4$ bytes = 64 KiB each: 128 KiB, half of an H100 SM's 256 KiB register file. Only $m$, $l$ and $L$ are vectors.

So tiles cannot simply grow. Doubling $B_c$ to 256 doubles $S_{ij}$ to 128 KiB of registers. The FlashAttention-2 paper notes that past a certain block size registers spill (overflow into slow local memory) or the kernel needs more shared memory than the GPU has and cannot run at all, so it typically uses blocks of $\{64, 128\} \times \{64, 128\}$. Larger tiles do help: every $K_j$, $V_j$ is read once per query tile, so a larger $B_r$ means fewer rereads (lesson 3 counts them).

**Causal masking.** In a decoder, query $i$ may only see keys $j \le i$. Working in tiles, the kernel skips every tile whose columns all lie above the diagonal and applies the mask only inside diagonal tiles; with square tiles that is one masked tile per query tile. With $T$ tiles per side it visits $T(T+1)/2$ of $T^2$ tiles. At $N = 8192$ with 128-wide tiles that is 2080 of 4096, 50.8%, which is why benchmark formulas halve the FLOPs for causal attention (lesson 3); the FlashAttention-2 paper measures about a 1.7 to 1.8x speedup from skipping. At $N = 512$ it is 10 of 16 tiles, 62.5%: short causal runs do more work than the halved formula credits.

blocks.question: A causal kernel with $B_r = B_c = 128$ processes a 512-token sequence, so query tiles $i$ and key tiles $j$ both run from 0 to 3. Which tiles $S_{ij}$ does it never load?
options: Every tile with $j < i$, because those keys were already processed
None: it loads every tile and multiplies the masked scores by zero
Only the diagonal tiles $i = j$, which are fully masked
Every tile with $j > i$: 6 of the 16 tiles
blocks.explain: Tiles above the diagonal ($j > i$) hold only masked scores, so $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$ of 16 are skipped and 10 are computed. Diagonal tiles are half valid, so they are loaded and masked inside. Loading masked tiles and zeroing them would give the right answer but waste exactly the work that skipping saves.

blocks.md: **Who does what.** The original FlashAttention ran one thread block per (batch, head) pair, with the loop over query tiles inside it. That fills the GPU only when batch times heads is large; the FlashAttention-2 paper names about 80 thread blocks for the 108 SMs of an A100. Long sequences usually come with small batches, so FlashAttention-2 also parallelizes over query tiles: the outer loop is embarrassingly parallel (no thread block needs another's result), so each query tile gets its own thread block. The paper credits Phil Tillet's Triton implementation with first ordering the loops this way and parallelizing over the sequence.

Inside a thread block the work is split across 4 or 8 warps. FlashAttention used **split-K**: each warp took a slice of $K_j$ and $V_j$, computed its slice of $Q_i K_j^\top$ and a partial $PV$ product, and then every warp wrote its partial result to shared memory, synchronized, and the partials were added up, on every iteration. FlashAttention-2 uses **split-Q**: each warp takes a slice of the rows of $Q_i$ and reads all of $K_j$ and $V_j$. A warp then owns complete rows of $S$ and $O_i$, so it needs nothing from the other warps.

blocks.title: Inside one thread block: split-K (FlashAttention) vs split-Q (FA2)

scenes.caption: Split-K: every warp reads all of $Q_i$ and a quarter of $K_j, V_j$. Each holds only part of every row, so partial outputs go through shared memory, all warps synchronize, and the partials are summed, every iteration.
Split-Q: every warp reads all of $K_j, V_j$ and a quarter of the rows of $Q_i$. It owns whole rows of $S$, so its row max, row sum and rows of $O_i$ are complete without talking to other warps.

blocks.md:
**Backward.** The backward pass receives $dO$ (the loss gradient with respect to $O$) and must produce $dQ$, $dK$ and $dV$. It needs $P$, which the forward pass did not store: at $N = 8192$ one head's $P$ is 128 MiB in FP16, while $L$ is 8192 FP32 values, 32 KiB. Because $L_i$ is the log of row $i$'s full softmax denominator, $P_{ij} = e^{S_{ij} - L_i}$ exactly, so the backward recomputes $S$ and $P$ tile by tile from $Q$, $K$ and $L$.

FlashAttention-2's backward swaps the loops: one thread block per key tile $j$, looping over query tiles $i$. For each pair it runs five matmuls: recompute $S_{ij} = Q_i K_j^\top$; add $P_{ij}^\top dO_i$ into $dV_j$; $dP_{ij} = dO_i V_j^\top$; then form $dS_{ij} = P_{ij} \circ (dP_{ij} - D_i)$ elementwise ($\circ$ is the elementwise product); add $dS_{ij}^\top Q_i$ into $dK_j$ and $dS_{ij} K_j$ into $dQ_i$. $dK_j$ and $dV_j$ stay on chip, but $dQ_i$ receives a piece from every key tile, so it is summed in HBM with atomic adds, indivisible read-add-write steps that no other thread block can interrupt (lesson 8 returns to this).

blocks.tex: dS_{ij} = P_{ij}\Big(dP_{ij} - \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_k P_{ik}\, dP_{ik}}_{D_i}\Big),\qquad D_i = \sum_k P_{ik}\,(dO_i \cdot v_k) = dO_i \cdot \sum_k P_{ik}\, v_k = dO_i \cdot O_i
blocks.caption: Left: the softmax Jacobian $\mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^\top$ applied to row $i$ of $dP$. Right: since $dP_{ik} = dO_i \cdot v_k$ and $O_i = \sum_k P_{ik} v_k$, the row sum $D_i$ needs only $O_i$ and $dO_i$ (derivation as in the FlashAttention paper's appendix).

blocks.md: So the backward starts with a cheap preprocessing step, $D = \mathrm{rowsum}(dO \circ O)$: $N \times d$ multiply-adds, instead of a reduction over whole rows of $P$ and $dP$, which no single thread block holds (each sees only its key tile). FlashAttention-3's Hopper code runs it as a separate kernel that reads $O$ and $dO$ and writes the result (called `dPsum` there) before the main loop. The script below checks the identity, and checks $dS$ itself against a finite difference of the loss.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, d = 6, 4
Q, K, V, dO = (rng.standard_normal((N, d)) for _ in range(4))

def softmax(S):
    P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return P / P.sum(1, keepdims=True)

S = Q @ K.T                      # 1/sqrt(d) left out, as in the papers
P = softmax(S); O = P @ V
dP = dO @ V.T                    # chain rule through O = P V
D_from_P = (P * dP).sum(1)       # needs whole rows of P and dP
D_from_O = (dO * O).sum(1)       # needs only O and dO: N*d work
print(np.allclose(D_from_P, D_from_O))
dS = P * (dP - D_from_O[:, None])

# finite-difference check of one entry, loss = sum(dO * O)
eps, (r, c) = 1e-6, (3, 1)
Sp, Sm = S.copy(), S.copy()
Sp[r, c] += eps; Sm[r, c] -= eps
num = ((dO * (softmax(Sp) @ V)).sum() - (dO * (softmax(Sm) @ V)).sum()) / (2 * eps)
print(round(dS[r, c], 6), round(num, 6))
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU with NumPy. Output: `True` (both ways of computing $D$ agree) and `0.03018 0.03018` (the formula for $dS$ matches the numerical derivative).

blocks.md: Every later kernel is this loop. FlashAttention-3's producer warps load $K_j, V_j$ and its pipeline overlaps the next $S_{ij}$ with the current $PV$; FlashAttention-4 moves $S$ and $P$ out of registers into a new on-chip memory, pairs thread blocks for the five backward matmuls, and orders causal tiles longest first (lessons 6 to 8). Only the mapping onto hardware changes.

blocks.question: In the backward pass a thread block holds key tile $j$, yet $dS$ needs $D_i = \sum_k P_{ik}\, dP_{ik}$ over all keys $k$ of row $i$. How does FlashAttention-2 get $D_i$?
options: A preprocessing step computes $D = \mathrm{rowsum}(dO \circ O)$, since $D_i = dO_i \cdot O_i$
Each thread block sums its own keys and the partial sums are combined with atomic adds before use
The forward pass stores $D$ next to $L$
It uses $D_i = 1$, because every row of $P$ sums to 1
blocks.explain: $D_i$ depends on $dO$, which does not exist during the forward pass, and partial sums would force a synchronization across thread blocks before any $dS$ could be formed. The identity $D_i = dO_i \cdot O_i$ makes it an $O(Nd)$ elementwise pass. Rows of $P$ do sum to 1, but $D_i$ weights each $P_{ik}$ by $dP_{ik}$.

lessons.title: Counting the work: FLOPs, bytes, and the exponential unit

blocks.md: The forward pass of one head does two matrix multiplies, $QK^\top$ and $PV$, each costing $2N^2d$ floating-point operations (FLOPs), where one FLOP is one multiply or one add. Why $2N^2d$: $QK^\top$ has $N^2$ entries, each a dot product of two length-$d$ vectors, which is $d$ multiplies and $d$ adds; $PV$ has $N \cdot d$ entries, each a length-$N$ dot product, again $2N^2d$ in total. The papers' benchmark formula is therefore $4 \cdot N^2 \cdot d \cdot \text{heads}$ FLOPs, halved for causal masking (only about half the scores are computed) and multiplied by 2.5 for the backward pass (5 matmuls instead of 2, because $S$ and $P$ are recomputed). Per query token that is $4Nd$ per head, the same $4 \times$ context $\times$ width per token that the *GPU and inference basics* course uses, summed over all $N$ query tokens.

Now the bytes for that same head in FP16 (2 bytes per element). Reading $Q, K, V$ and writing $O$ is $4 \cdot N \cdot d \cdot 2 = 8$ MiB. A naive kernel also writes $S$, reads it back for the softmax, writes $P$ and reads it for $PV$: four passes over 128 MiB each.

blocks.title: HBM traffic for one head, N = 8192, d = 128 (MiB)
labels: Q, K, V in + O out

scenes.caption: Naive attention: 8 MiB of real inputs and outputs, plus 512 MiB of intermediate traffic. The intermediates are 98% of the bytes.

Fused, tiled attention (every FlashAttention version): $S$ and $P$ live only on chip. The ideal traffic is the 8 MiB of unique inputs and outputs. Simplified: real kernels re-read K and V tiles for each query block.

Counting rereads: each of the 64 query tiles ($B_r = 128$) reads all of K and V, 4 MiB, so 256 MiB plus 4 MiB for Q and O. Half the naive traffic if every byte came from HBM; in practice most rereads hit L2.

blocks.md: Divide FLOPs by bytes to get **arithmetic intensity**. The naive kernel moves 8 + 512 = 520 MiB, about $545 \times 10^6$ bytes, so it does $34.4 \times 10^9 / 545 \times 10^6 \approx 63$ FLOPs per byte; the fused kernel's ideal is $4N^2d / 8Nd = N/2 = 4096$. The H100's **ridge point**, its peak FLOP rate divided by its memory bandwidth, is $989 \text{ TFLOPS} / 3.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295$ FLOPs per byte. Below it a kernel spends longer moving bytes than doing math (memory bound); above it the math units are the limit (compute bound). So the naive kernel is memory bound and the fused kernel is, on paper, compute bound. (FlashAttention's IO analysis counts the K and V re-reads as $\Theta(N^2 d^2 / M)$ HBM accesses for on-chip memory size $M$, still far below $\Theta(N^2)$.)

The ideal $N/2$ assumes each byte of K and V crosses HBM once. The tiled kernel actually rereads K and V once per query tile (lesson 2): with $B_r = 128$ there are $8192/128 = 64$ query tiles, each reading K and V, $2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 128 \cdot 2$ bytes = 4 MiB, so 256 MiB plus 4 MiB for Q and O. If every one of those bytes came from HBM, the intensity would be $34.4 \times 10^9 / 272.6 \times 10^6 \approx 126$ FLOPs per byte, below the ridge of 295: memory bound. In practice the query tiles of one head run at about the same time on different SMs and share K and V through the 50 MB L2 cache, which holds a head's 4 MiB of K and V many times over, so most rereads never reach HBM. That is why the order in which tiles are scheduled matters (the L2-aware swizzling in lesson 8).

blocks.prompt: FlashAttention-2 already removes the $N^2$ HBM traffic, so attention should run near the tensor-core peak. On an H100, what fraction of the 989 TFLOPS FP16 peak did the FlashAttention-3 authors measure for FlashAttention-2?
blocks.reveal: **About 35%**, versus 80 to 90% for well-tuned matrix multiplies on the same GPU. Being compute bound in the roofline sense is not enough: the kernel also has to keep the tensor cores fed every cycle. FlashAttention-2 uses a synchronous design (its matmul instructions make the issuing warp wait for the result) and instructions from Ampere, NVIDIA's previous GPU generation (the A100, 2020), and it pays for the softmax's slow operations in series with the matmuls.

blocks.md: The slow operations are the non-matmul ones, above all the exponential. On the H100, exponentials run on the **multi-function unit (MUFU)**, a separate unit for functions such as exp, log and sine, at 16 operations per clock per streaming multiprocessor (SM). Times 132 SMs and 1.83 GHz that is 3.9 TFLOPS, against 989 TFLOPS of FP16 matmul: a 256x gap. The 989 is $132 \times 1.83 \times 10^9 \times 4096$: per SM per clock the tensor cores do 4096 FLOPs to MUFU's 16 exponentials, and $4096/16 = 256$.

Each score costs one exponential but $4d = 512$ matmul FLOPs at $d = 128$: $2d$ for its dot product in $QK^\top$, and $2d$ when its weight multiplies a length-$d$ row of $V$ and is added into $O$. One exponential takes as long as 256 matmul FLOPs, so the exponentials need $256/512 = 0.5$ of the matmul time.

In general, write $r_{MMA}$ for the tensor cores' FLOPs per clock per SM, named for the matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA), their basic operation, which computes $D = AB + C$ for operand tiles A and B, and $r_{exp}$ for MUFU's exponentials per clock per SM. The $N^2$ exponentials take $N^2 / r_{exp}$ clocks and the $4N^2d$ FLOPs take $4N^2d / r_{MMA}$; dividing, $N^2$ cancels and the ratio is $r_{MMA} / (4 d\, r_{exp})$.

blocks.caption: Per SM per clock: H100 $r_{MMA} = 4096$, $r_{exp} = 16$, so at $d = 128$ the ratio is $4096/8192 = 0.5$. B200 doubles $r_{MMA}$ to 8192 and keeps $r_{exp} = 16$: ratio 1.0.

blocks.title: Exponential time as a fraction of matmul time

params.name: r
params.label: exp ops per clock per SM

scenes.caption: With 16 exp ops per clock per SM (H100 and B200), at $d = 128$ the exponentials cost 0.5 of the matmul time on H100 and 1.0 on B200. If they run in series with the matmuls, they cap utilization.
The FlashAttention-4 paper notes B300/GB300 double MUFU to 32 ops per clock per SM, which halves the curves. Smaller head dimensions are worse: less matmul work per exponential.

blocks.md: Misconception: "attention is two GEMMs, so it runs at GEMM speed." The softmax between them is cheap in FLOPs but runs on units hundreds of times slower than the tensor cores. FP8 makes it worse: matmul throughput doubles while exponential throughput stays the same.

blocks.title: Reported best forward throughput as % of dense peak

scenes.caption: Utilization = reported TFLOPs/s divided by the stated peak: 230/312 = 73.7% on A100, about 35% on H100 (as reported), 740/989 = 74.8% for FA3, 1613/2250 = 71.7% for FA4. Each new GPU resets the kernel back to low utilization until it is redesigned.

blocks.question: On H100 at $d = 128$, exponentials take about 50% of the matmul time. If FP8 matmuls run at 2x the FP16 rate and MUFU is unchanged, what does that ratio become?
options: 25%, because FP8 values are half the size
50%, unchanged
About 100%
About 200%
blocks.explain: $T_{exp}/T_{MMA} = r_{MMA}/(4 d\, r_{exp})$. Doubling $r_{MMA}$ doubles the ratio from 0.5 to 1.0: the exponentials now take as long as the matmuls. The FlashAttention-3 paper says exactly this: "the matmul throughput doubles but the exponential throughput stays the same."

blocks.question: Why is the fused kernel's ideal arithmetic intensity $N/2$ FLOPs per byte rather than a constant?
options: Because FLOPs grow as $N^2 d$ while unique bytes (Q, K, V, O) grow only as $N d$
Because longer sequences use larger tiles
Because the softmax is cheaper for long rows
Because HBM bandwidth increases with $N$
blocks.explain: $4N^2 d$ FLOPs over $8Nd$ bytes (4 matrices, 2 bytes each) is $N/2$. The naive kernel instead moves $\Theta(N^2)$ bytes for $\Theta(N^2 d)$ FLOPs, so its intensity is stuck near a constant (about $d/2$), which is why it stays memory bound at every length.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong

blocks.md: FlashAttention-3 (Shah, Bikshandi, Zhang, Thakkar, Ramani and Dao, 2024) targets the Hopper H100 (Hopper is NVIDIA's GPU generation after Ampere, launched in 2022). Three Hopper features matter. The **Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA)** is a hardware unit that copies tiles between HBM and the 228 KiB per-SM shared memory (SMEM) asynchronously: the thread that issues a copy does not wait for it and can go on working. **WGMMA** (warpgroup matrix multiply-accumulate) is Hopper's tensor-core instruction: it is issued by a **warpgroup** (4 warps, 128 threads), reads operand B straight from SMEM (operand A from SMEM or from registers), and runs asynchronously, so the issuing threads can keep working. And **setmaxnreg** (set maximum number of registers) lets warpgroups give registers to each other at run time. Registers are each thread's private, fastest storage, and their number per thread is normally fixed when the kernel is compiled.

**What asynchronous changes.** On Ampere, the tensor-core instruction is the warp-level `mma.sync`: one warp multiplies a small tile (for example $16 \times 8 \times 16$) whose operands and result live in that warp's registers, so the same warps must first copy data from shared memory into registers and then wait for the result before they can use it. Hopper's `wgmma.mma_async` is issued by a whole warpgroup on a tile 64 rows tall, reads operand B from shared memory (operand A from shared memory or registers), and runs in the background; the warpgroup waits only when it executes `wgmma.wait_group`, which blocks until the chosen earlier groups of MMAs are complete. TMA does the same for copies. The *CUTLASS and CuTe* course covers TMA, multistage pipelines and warp specialization for GEMMs in general; this lesson covers what FlashAttention-3 does with them.

Asynchrony enables **warp specialization**: a thread block's warps are split into roles that only ever issue one kind of work. In FlashAttention-3, a **producer** warpgroup issues TMA loads of the $K_j$ and $V_j$ tiles into an $s$-stage circular buffer in SMEM ($s$ tile-sized slots reused in a ring), and **consumer** warpgroups issue WGMMAs and do the softmax. Barriers say when a stage is full (consumer may read) and when it is free again (producer may overwrite).

blocks.title: Producer and consumer sharing a 2-stage SMEM buffer

scenes.caption: The producer frees most of its registers (one thread is enough to issue TMA) and starts loads for $Q_i$ (into its own buffer, outside the ring) and the first $K$, $V$ tiles. It does not wait for any load to finish before issuing the next.

add.label: TMA: Q_i, K0, V0 to stage 0

scenes.caption: When a load lands, a barrier tells the consumer stage 0 is full. The consumer, which received the extra registers, runs $S = Q_i K_0^\top$ as an SS-GEMM (both operands from SMEM).
Done with $K_0, V_0$, the consumer releases stage 0. Only then may the producer reuse it, here for $K_2, V_2$. Meanwhile stage 1 is already loaded, so the consumer never waits on HBM.
At the end the consumer divides by $l$, computes $L = m + \log l$ and writes $O_i$ and $L_i$ to HBM. Loads and math overlapped the whole time, with no warp doing both.

add.label: O = O / l, L = m + log l

blocks.md: Why move registers? The producer only issues TMA, for which a single thread suffices, while consumers hold the $S$ and $O$ accumulators (the matmul outputs, whose running sums stay in registers). setmaxnreg shifts the register budget to the warps that do math, which allows larger tiles.

**The budget, with real numbers.** For head dimension 128 in BF16, the repo's Hopper tile table picks $B_r = 128$ query rows, $B_c = 176$ keys (128 when causal) and 2 pipeline stages. Shared memory holds $Q_i$, $128 \times 128 \times 2$ bytes = 32 KiB, plus two stages of $K_j$ and $V_j$ at $176 \times 128 \times 2$ bytes = 44 KiB each, 176 KiB: 208 KiB in total, against the 227 KiB (NVIDIA writes 227 KB) a single thread block may use on an H100. A third stage would add 88 KiB and cannot fit; the table's comments note that $128 \times 192$ tiles (224 KiB) already sit at the shared memory limit. So 2 stages is not a matter of taste: it is what is left once the tiles are as large as possible.

Registers are tighter. An H100 SM has 64K 32-bit registers (256 KiB), and a thread may use at most 255. This thread block has 3 warpgroups, 384 threads: split evenly, at most 170 registers each (168 in practice, since registers are allocated in steps of 8). Each consumer warpgroup owns 64 of the 128 query rows, so per thread it holds a $64 \times 176$ FP32 score tile (88 registers), a $64 \times 128$ FP32 output accumulator (64) and $P$ in BF16 as the next matmul's register operand (44): 196 before addresses, softmax statistics and temporaries (a count from the tile shapes, not a compiler report). With setmaxnreg the code drops the producer to 24 registers per thread and raises both consumers to 240: $128 \cdot 24 + 256 \cdot 240 = 64{,}512$ of 65,536.

blocks.title: FA3 thread block budget, d = 128, BF16, 128 x 176 tiles (KiB)

scenes.caption: Shared memory: 208 KiB of the 227 KiB a block may use. Registers split evenly (170 per thread): 85 KiB for the producer, 170 KiB for both consumers, too few per consumer thread for its tiles.
With setmaxnreg: the producer keeps 24 registers per thread (12 KiB), the consumers get 240 each (240 KiB for both). Almost the same 256 KiB total, moved to where the matmuls are.

blocks.md: Warp specialization overlaps loads with math. It does not overlap the softmax with the matmuls of the same warpgroup. **Ping-pong scheduling** does that across two consumer warpgroups: named barriers (`bar.sync`, a hardware barrier with an id, where only the warps using that id wait) force warpgroup 1's GEMMs (PV of this iteration plus $QK^\top$ of the next) to issue before warpgroup 2's. So warpgroup 1 runs its softmax while warpgroup 2 occupies the tensor cores, then the roles swap. The idea is adapted from the ping-pong GEMM of CUTLASS, NVIDIA's open-source C++ template library for matrix multiply kernels.

blocks.title: Simplified model: GEMM = 1 unit each, softmax = 1 unit

scenes.caption: One consumer, no overlap: QK, then softmax, then PV. Softmax costs half of the two GEMMs (the H100 ratio at $d = 128$), so the tensor cores sit idle 4 of every 12 units: 67% busy.

Ping-pong with two warpgroups: each warpgroup's softmax runs while the other's GEMMs hold the tensor cores. In this idealized model they stay 100% busy and finish 12 GEMM units in the time the serial schedule did 8.

blocks.md: The real gain is smaller than the idealized model because instruction issue, barriers and register limits get in the way. The paper reports that ping-pong took FP16 forward at head dimension 128 and sequence length 8192 from 570 TFLOPs/s to 620 to 640 TFLOPs/s, from 57.6% to about 63 to 65% of the 989 TFLOPS peak. That is one step, reported as a range, not two successive improvements.

blocks.title: Tensor cores busy vs softmax-to-GEMM time ratio

y.label: fraction of time tensor cores busy

scenes.caption: Simplified model (not from the paper): one warpgroup alternates its GEMMs and softmax, so the tensor cores are busy $1/(1+r)$. With two, each softmax hides under the other's GEMMs, until two softmaxes on the shared MUFU fill the time: $\min(1, 1/r)$.

At $r = 0.5$ (H100, BF16, $d = 128$, lesson 3) ping-pong has slack. At $r = 1$ (B200 BF16, or FP8 on H100) the ideal schedule has none, so every stall shows up directly. That is the gap FlashAttention-4 attacks.

blocks.question: In ping-pong scheduling, what is warpgroup 2 doing while warpgroup 1 computes its softmax?
options: Waiting at a barrier until warpgroup 1 finishes
Running its GEMMs (PV of one iteration and QK of the next) on the tensor cores
Issuing TMA loads for the next K and V tiles
Computing its own softmax on the multi-function unit
blocks.explain: The barriers order the two warpgroups' GEMMs so that one warpgroup's slow softmax (exp on MUFU) lands under the other's tensor-core work. Loading is the producer warpgroup's job, and running both softmaxes at once would just make them compete for MUFU.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
blocks.explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately

blocks.md: Within one warpgroup the loop body is a dependency chain: softmax needs $S_j = Q_i K_j^\top$, and $P_j V_j$ needs the softmax output. FlashAttention-3 breaks the chain by pipelining **across** iterations. Because WGMMA is asynchronous, the warpgroup can issue $Q_i K_{j}^\top$ for the next block and $\tilde P_{cur} V_{j-1}$ for the previous one ($\tilde P_{cur}$ holds the previous block's softmax weights; the tilde means not yet divided by $l$), then run the softmax on the new scores while the $PV$ GEMM is still executing on the tensor cores.

blocks.code:
# Consumer warpgroup, 2-stage pipeline (simplified from Algorithm 2)
S_cur = wgmma(Q_i, K[0]); wait()
m, P_cur, l = softmax_step(S_cur)
for j in range(1, Tc):
    S_next = wgmma(Q_i, K[j])        # issue, do not wait
    O = O + wgmma(P_cur, V[j-1])     # issue, do not wait
    wait(S_next)
    m, P_next, l = softmax_step(S_next)  # overlaps the PV GEMM
    wait(O); O = rescale(O)
    release(K[j], V[j-1])
    P_cur = P_next
O = O + wgmma(P_cur, V[Tc-1]); wait()
O = O / l
blocks.caption: Paraphrase of the paper's Algorithm 2; real code also handles masking, FP32 to FP16 conversion and barriers.

blocks.title: One warpgroup, 4 iterations: serial vs 2-stage pipeline

scenes.caption: Serial: each iteration costs 3 units (QK, softmax, PV) and 4 iterations take 12. Simplified model with every step costing 1 unit.

2-stage: softmax of block $j$ runs while PV of block $j-1$ is on the tensor cores. Each steady-state iteration costs 2 units, so the same work ends at 9. Idealized: the compiler must not undo the ordering.

blocks.md: The overlap is not free. The pipeline keeps an extra $S_{next}$ in registers, $B_r \times B_c \times 4$ bytes per thread block (one FP32 score per entry): with $B_r = B_c = 128$ that is 64 KiB, a quarter of the SM's 256 KiB register file. That competes with large tiles, which are also register hungry. The authors also tried a 3-stage version; it needed even more registers and the compiler only overlapped one of the two GEMMs, so it performed worse than 2-stage.

blocks.title: Ablation: FP16, batch 4, seqlen 8448, 16 heads, d = 128

scenes.caption: Removing either technique costs 12 to 14%: 570 and 582 vs 661 TFLOPs/s, or 57.6%, 58.8% and 66.8% of the 989 TFLOPS peak. Check: $4 \cdot 8448^2 \cdot 128 \cdot 16 \cdot 4 / 3.538\text{ ms} = 661$. The headline 740 (75%) comes from other shapes.

blocks.md:
**FP8.** A floating-point number stores a sign, exponent bits (which set the power of two) and mantissa bits (the digits after the leading 1, which set the precision). FP16 has 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits; BF16 (bfloat16), the "brain float" format from Google Brain, keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits with 7 mantissa bits; the FP8 format used here, **e4m3**, has 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits. With 3 mantissa bits there are only 8 steps between consecutive powers of two (between 1 and 2: 1, 1.125, 1.25 and so on), and the largest e4m3 value is $1.75 \times 2^8 = 448$.

The *FP8 and FP4 training* course covers these formats, E5M2 and scaling recipes in depth; here only what attention needs. Hopper's FP8 tensor cores have twice the FP16 throughput per SM. Two problems follow.

First, layout: FP8 WGMMA requires operands contiguous in the inner (k) dimension, the one the matmul sums over. For $PV$ that is the key position, but V is usually stored contiguous in the head dimension (each key's $d$ values side by side), so FlashAttention-3 transposes each V tile inside the kernel with the LDSM and STSM instructions (load and store a matrix between shared memory and registers), and permutes the registers of the first GEMM's FP32 accumulator so it can feed the second GEMM. Second, accuracy: FP8 e4m3 has only 3 mantissa bits, and LLM activations have **outliers**, a few entries far larger than the rest.

Two techniques fix the accuracy. To quantize, the kernel divides a block of numbers by a **scale** chosen so its largest magnitude lands near 448, rounds to FP8, and multiplies the scale back in after the matmul. One huge outlier forces a large scale, which pushes the ordinary entries far down the range, and those that fall below e4m3's smallest normal value ($2^{-6}$) lose mantissa bits or round to zero. **Block quantization** keeps one scale per $B_r \times d$ or $B_c \times d$ block of Q, K and V instead of one per tensor, and since the kernel works on blocks anyway, applying the scales costs nothing. **Incoherent processing** multiplies Q and K by the same random orthogonal matrix $M$ (a rotation or reflection) before quantizing. Because $MM^\top = I$, the scores are unchanged, but each entry of $QM$ is a mix of many entries, so an outlier gets spread out.

FlashAttention-3 uses a Hadamard matrix times a random $\pm 1$ diagonal, which costs $O(d \log d)$ and can be fused into the rotary embedding. A **Hadamard matrix** has only $+1$ and $-1$ entries and mutually orthogonal rows; it is built by doubling ($H_{2n}$ puts $H_n$ beside $H_n$ on top and $H_n$ beside $-H_n$ below), and scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$ it is orthogonal. That recursive structure lets $xH$ be computed in $\log_2 d$ rounds of $d$ additions or subtractions, like a fast Fourier transform: 896 operations at $d = 128$ instead of $128^2 = 16384$ for a general matrix. The random signs make the rotation random. The **rotary embedding** (RoPE) is the step that already rotates pairs of query and key coordinates by position-dependent angles to encode each token's position, so the extra multiply rides along with it.

blocks.caption: Incoherent processing does not change attention scores, only how they are quantized.

blocks.title: A query with an outlier, before and after a 4x4 rotation

scenes.caption: Original vectors. $q$ has one outlier (8.0) and three small entries, so one entry sets the shared FP8 scale. Max/RMS (largest magnitude over root mean square: 1 if all are equal, at most 2 for 4 entries) of $q$ is 1.99. Toy numbers.
After $M = DH$ (a $\pm 1$ diagonal times the normalized 4x4 Hadamard): $qM = (4.3, -4, -3.5, 4.2)$, max/RMS 1.07, so every entry uses the FP8 range well. $kM = (0.7, 0.3, -0.4, 0.2)$.
The dot product is preserved: $q \cdot k = 4.05$ and $(qM)\cdot(kM) = 4.05$. Attention scores are unchanged before quantization; only the rounding error changes.

blocks.title: FP8 attention RMSE vs FP64 reference (x 0.001, outlier test)

scenes.caption: Inputs are $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ plus a rare $\mathcal{N}(0,100)$ outlier term on 0.1% of entries. RMSE is root mean squared error. FA3 FP8 reaches 9.1e-3 vs 24e-3 for the baseline: $24/9.1 = 2.6$x lower error.
The ablations show which part matters on this test: dropping block quantization barely changes the error (9.3e-3), while dropping incoherent processing returns it to the baseline (24e-3).

blocks.md: FP8 FlashAttention-3 was released for the forward pass only (FP16 and BF16 have forward and backward), and the paper's FP8 kernel lacked the persistent-kernel load balancing of the FP16 one (about one long-lived thread block per SM, looping over tiles), so it trailed the FP8 kernels of cuDNN (NVIDIA's deep learning library) for short sequences and causal masking. It reached close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s, about 60% of an FP8 peak taken as twice the FP16 peak.

blocks.question: Why does multiplying both Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix reduce FP8 error without changing the attention output?
options: It shrinks every value toward zero, so rounding errors are smaller
Scores are preserved because $MM^\top = I$, and mixing entries spreads outliers so one scale fits all entries better
It sorts the head dimension so outliers end up in a single block that is kept in FP16
It converts the values to integers, which FP8 represents exactly
blocks.explain: Orthogonality keeps $QK^\top$ identical. Each rotated entry is a signed sum of many original entries, which evens out magnitudes (max/RMS fell from 1.99 to 1.07 in the toy example), so quantization with a shared scale loses less information.

blocks.question: Your FA3-style kernel (head dimension 128, consumers at 240 registers) spills after you enlarge the key block size $B_c$ from 176 to 256. Which part of the 2-stage pipeline is most directly to blame?
options: The extra $S_{next}$ buffer of $B_r \times B_c$ FP32 values kept in registers
The TMA descriptors, which grow with $B_c$
The circular SMEM buffer, which lives in registers
The log-sum-exp vector, which grows with $B_c$
blocks.explain: The paper calls out exactly this tradeoff: the 2-stage pipeline holds an extra $S_{next}$ of size $B_r \times B_c \times$ sizeof(float) per thread block, which competes with larger block sizes. SMEM buffers are not in registers, and the log-sum-exp has one value per query row ($B_r$), not per key.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck

blocks.md: FlashAttention-4 (Zadouri, Hoehnerbach, Shah, Liu, Thakkar and Dao, 2026) targets Blackwell B200 and GB200 (Blackwell is NVIDIA's generation after Hopper; a GB200 pairs two B200 GPUs with a Grace CPU). Its premise is **asymmetric scaling**: B200 BF16 tensor cores do 8192 ops per clock per SM, twice Hopper's 4096 (2.25 vs about 1 PFLOPS per GPU; the paper derives 8192 as 2.25 PFLOPS over 148 SMs at 1.85 GHz), while MUFU stays at 16 exponentials per clock per SM and shared memory reads stay at 128 bytes per clock per SM. FlashAttention-3 does not run on B200 at all: Hopper's WGMMA instructions are not forward compatible.

Blackwell also brings new hardware. **Tensor memory (TMEM)** is 256 KB per SM of on-chip storage wired to the tensor cores, so MMA results land there instead of in registers. The 5th-generation MMA (`tcgen05.mma`) is fully asynchronous, launched by a single thread, works on tiles of 128 rows (vs 64 rows on Hopper), and can read operand A from TMEM. A **2-CTA** mode lets two thread blocks, or cooperative thread arrays (CTAs), the hardware's name for a thread block, in a **cluster** execute one MMA together. A cluster, added in Hopper, is a group of thread blocks that run at the same time on nearby SMs and can read and write each other's shared memory, which is then called distributed shared memory (DSMEM).

The paper starts with a per-tile roofline ("feeds and speeds"): for one tile, count the clock cycles each unit (tensor cores, shared memory, MUFU) needs; the busiest unit sets the time. For a query tile of $M$ rows, a key tile of $N$ columns (the $B_r$ and $B_c$ of lesson 2; here $N$ is the tile's width, not the sequence length) and head dimension $d$, all multiples of 128:

blocks.caption: Shared-memory time counts operands re-read by multiple 128-wide MMA instructions, at 2 bytes per element and 128 bytes per cycle.

blocks.md: Where each term comes from. The tile does two matmuls of $2MNd$ FLOPs each at 8192 per cycle: $4MNd/8192$. It needs one exponential per score, $MN$ of them, at 16 per cycle: $MN/16$. Shared memory feeds the MMAs: each $128 \times 128$ piece of $S$ reads a $128 \times d$ chunk of Q and of K, and each $128 \times 128$ piece of $O$ reads an $N \times 128$ chunk of V ($P$ comes from TMEM). At 2 bytes per element and 128 bytes per cycle that sums to $3MNd/8192$. At $M = N = d = 128$: 32,768 elements of Q and K plus 16,384 of V is 98,304 bytes, or 768 cycles.

blocks.title: B200 forward roofline per tile (clock cycles)

scenes.caption: $M = N = d = 128$: MMA $4 \cdot 128^3/8192 = 1024$, SMEM 768, exp $128^2/16 = 1024$. The exponentials take as long as both matmuls together, so any serialization halves throughput.
$M = 256$ (two 128-row query tiles): 2048, 1536 and 2048. Larger tiles do not change the balance; exp still ties the tensor cores.

Illustrative, not from the paper: if 20% of the exponentials move to the FMA units (FP32 units computing $a \times b + c$; FA4 emulates 10 to 25%), MUFU work for the 128 tile drops from 1024 to 819 cycles, under the MMA time.

blocks.md: **The pipeline.** Each CTA computes two 128-row query tiles, $Q^H$ and $Q^L$, in ping-pong as in FlashAttention-3. Because the $128 \times 128$ score tile sits in TMEM and is read out one row per thread, each 128-thread softmax warpgroup owns one tile, with one full row per thread, so no shuffles (instructions that pass register values between threads of a warp) are needed for the row max. The two softmax warpgroups are synchronized so their exponential phases do not overlap. $P$ goes back to TMEM in stages (three quarters, then the last quarter) to limit register pressure, and the PV MMA starts as soon as the first chunk is stored.

blocks.title: FlashAttention-4 forward: warp roles in one CTA

scenes.caption: TMA brings K and V tiles into SMEM; a single thread launches MMAs whose results go to TMEM, not registers. That freed register file is what makes 128-element rows per thread affordable.
The two softmax warpgroups read rows of S from TMEM, compute exponentials, and write P back for the PV MMA. They take turns on the exponential phase so they do not fight over MUFU.
A dedicated correction warpgroup rescales $O$ in TMEM when the running max changes, which takes rescaling off the softmax critical path. At the end it normalizes and writes $O$ and $L$.

blocks.md: **Counting the registers.** One row of a $128 \times 128$ FP32 score tile is 128 registers, and its row of $P$ in BF16 packs two values per register, 64 more: 192 of the at most 255 a thread may use, which is the paper's count. The thread block has 512 threads (two softmax warpgroups, a correction warpgroup, and a fourth holding the MMA, load and epilogue warps), so its 65,536 registers average 128 per thread. The repo's fallback split raises each softmax thread to 192 and leaves 80 for correction and 48 for the rest ($192 + 192 + 80 + 48 = 512$, one per-thread count for each of the 4 warpgroups); its tuning table overrides it for most tuned head-dimension-128 cases on B200, for example 184 and 80, or 192 and 64, with the rest getting what is left. On Hopper the output accumulator would sit in those registers too, 128 more per thread, 320 in all, which cannot fit. Because `tcgen05.mma` writes $S$ and $O$ to TMEM, a softmax thread only holds its row while working on it, and storing $P$ in two parts (three quarters, then a quarter) trims the peak further.

The exponential still ties the tensor cores in this roofline, and every rescale of $O$ is extra work for the correction warpgroup. The next lesson covers FlashAttention-4's two numerical answers: computing some exponentials on the FMA units, and skipping most rescales.

blocks.question: A Blackwell softmax thread owns one full 128-element row of the FP32 score tile, plus that row of $P$ in BF16. If the row of the FP32 output accumulator ($d = 128$) also had to stay in its registers, as Hopper accumulators do, how many registers would that take?
options: 192, which fits comfortably
64, because BF16 values pack two per register
128, because S and O can share registers
320, more than the 255 a thread can have
blocks.explain: 128 for the FP32 scores, 64 for $P$ packed two per register, and 128 for the FP32 output row: 320. A thread can use at most 255, so this layout only works because tensor memory holds $S$ and $O$ and the thread borrows one row at a time. Sharing registers between $S$ and $O$ is impossible while both are live.

blocks.question: According to the per-tile roofline, which resources bound the B200 forward pass at $M = N = d = 128$?
options: Shared memory bandwidth alone
HBM bandwidth

blocks.explain: MMA and exp are both 1024 cycles; shared memory is 768. This is why the forward pass's design centers on overlapping softmax with MMA and on reducing exp and rescaling work. Shared memory becomes the bottleneck in the backward pass.

lessons.title: FlashAttention-4 math tricks: software exp2, conditional rescaling

blocks.md: The last lesson's roofline left the exponential unit tied with the tensor cores at 1024 cycles per tile. FlashAttention-4 attacks it from two sides: compute some of the exponentials on other units, and skip work that only exists to keep exponentials small. A tiny example of the second: in lesson 1's row, block 3 did not raise the max, so its correction factor was exactly 1 and a rescale would have been wasted work. This lesson covers both tricks, with a script that reproduces the paper's accuracy numbers on a CPU.

**Software exponential.** The hardware exponential unit computes powers of 2, so kernels compute $e^x$ as $2^{x \log_2 e}$ (because $e = 2^{\log_2 e}$), and FlashAttention-4 evaluates some of those $2^x$ on the FMA units, which would otherwise idle, in parallel with MUFU. It uses Cody-Waite range reduction (from William Cody and William Waite's 1980 manual on computing elementary functions): shrink the input to a small range where a short polynomial is accurate.

Here that is $2^x = 2^{\lfloor x \rfloor} \cdot 2^{x - \lfloor x \rfloor}$. A float is stored as a mantissa times a power of 2, so the integer part just becomes exponent bits, and only the fractional part, in $[0, 1)$, needs a degree-3 polynomial, evaluated with Horner's method: start from $c_3$, then three times multiply by $f$ and add the next coefficient ($c_2$, then $c_1$, then $c_0$), one FMA per step. The coefficients come from the Sollya tool, which computes polynomial approximations of functions with small maximum error over a range.

blocks.title: Emulated 2^x for the score s - m = -2
blocks.code:
def exp2_emulated(x):
    x = max(x, -127.0)        # avoid underflow
    n = floor(x)              # GPU: add 2^23 + 2^22, round down
    f = x - n                 # fractional part in [0, 1)
    p = ((0.0771*f + 0.2276)*f + 0.6951)*f + 1.0
    return ldexp(p, n)        # shift n into the exponent bits

scenes.caption: The score $-2$ from lesson 1 (block 1's 1 minus max 3) becomes $x = -2 \log_2 e = -2.8854$, so we want $2^x = e^{-2} = 0.135335$.
Range reduction: $n = -3$ and $f = 0.1146$, so only $2^f$ on $[0, 1)$ needs a polynomial.
Three fused multiply-adds evaluate the polynomial. Coefficients rounded to 4 digits here; the code uses full FP32 values.

Putting $n$ into the exponent gives 0.135346, a relative error of $8.2 \times 10^{-5}$, far below BF16's own rounding step of about $3.9 \times 10^{-3}$ ($2^{-8}$, half of the $2^{-7}$ relative spacing that 7 mantissa bits give).

blocks.md: The paper measures the degree-3 polynomial at a maximum relative error of $8.8 \times 10^{-5}$ in FP32, about 600x worse than MUFU, but after rounding to BF16 the two are indistinguishable (within 1 BF16 ulp, unit in the last place, one step between adjacent BF16 values, on 99% of inputs). Emulation costs registers and latency, so only 10 to 25% of each row is emulated; the rest still uses `MUFU.EX2`, the MUFU instruction for $2^x$. The repo's tuning table sets this split per configuration.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from ml_dtypes import bfloat16
f32 = np.float32
# degree-3 coefficients from flash_attn/cute/utils.py (POLY_EX2[3])
c1, c2, c3 = f32(0.695146143436431884765625), f32(0.227564394474029541015625), f32(0.077119089663028717041015625)

def exp2_emulated(x):
    x = np.maximum(x.astype(f32), f32(-127))
    n = np.floor(x)                      # integer part
    f = x - n                            # fractional part in [0, 1)
    p = ((c3 * f + c2) * f + c1) * f + f32(1)   # Horner: 3 multiply-adds
    return np.ldexp(p, n.astype(np.int32))      # n goes into the exponent

x = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(0, 1, 4_000_000).astype(f32)
exact = np.exp2(x.astype(np.float64))
approx = exp2_emulated(x)
rel = np.abs(approx - exact) / exact
print(f"FP32 max rel err {rel.max():.3g}, mean {rel.mean():.3g}")

bf_exact = exact.astype(bfloat16).astype(np.float64)    # ideal BF16 result
bf_approx = approx.astype(bfloat16).astype(np.float64)
rel_bf = np.abs(bf_approx - exact) / exact
print(f"BF16 max rel err {rel_bf.max():.3g}, mean {rel_bf.mean():.3g}")
ulp = 2.0 ** (np.floor(np.log2(exact)) - 7)              # BF16 spacing here
print("same BF16 value as ideal:", f"{np.mean(bf_approx == bf_exact):.2%}")
print("within 1 BF16 ulp:", f"{np.mean(np.abs(bf_approx - bf_exact) <= ulp):.2%}")
x = np.float32(-2 * np.log2(np.e))
print(exp2_emulated(np.array([x]))[0], np.exp(-2.0))

blocks.md: The FP32 and BF16 numbers match the degree-3 row of the paper's accuracy table ($8.77 \times 10^{-5}$ and $5.43 \times 10^{-5}$ before rounding, $3.90 \times 10^{-3}$ and $1.41 \times 10^{-3}$ after). The paper compares against the hardware `MUFU.EX2`; without a GPU, this script compares against the exactly rounded BF16 value instead: 99.01% of inputs round to the same BF16 number, and every input is within one BF16 step of it. That is the sense in which a polynomial 600x less accurate in FP32 is as good as hardware for BF16 attention. With full coefficients $e^{-2}$ comes out as 0.135347 (the trace above used 4-digit coefficients). NumPy rounds after each multiply and each add, while the GPU uses fused multiply-adds, so last bits can differ slightly.

**Conditional rescaling.** Rescaling $O$ is only needed when the max grows, and a little slack is harmless as long as the final division uses consistent statistics. FlashAttention-4 rescales only when the max jumps by more than a threshold $\tau$; otherwise it keeps the old max. The code tracks the max in base-2 exponents, so a jump of $\Delta$ in the scores is $\Delta \log_2 e$ there, and it sets $\tau = 8$ in these log2 units (a factor of $2^8 = 256$) for 16-bit inputs and 0 for FP8, and the decision is made per warp to avoid divergence (if the threads of one warp took different branches, the warp would run both paths one after the other).

blocks.tex: O_j = \begin{cases} e^{m_{j-1}-m_j}\, O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_j} V_j & \text{if } m_j - m_{j-1} > \tau \\ O_{j-1} + e^{S_j - m_{j-1}} V_j & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: From the FlashAttention-4 paper (the code compares the jump in log2 units). In words: if the max grew by more than $\tau$, rescale as in plain online softmax; otherwise leave $O$ as it is and take the new block's exponentials against the old max.

blocks.md: **Why skipping is exact.** Call $\tilde m$ whatever reference the kernel is currently subtracting. Every term added to $l$ and $O$ is $e^{s - \tilde m}$, so $l = e^{-\tilde m}\sum_k e^{s_k}$ and $O = e^{-\tilde m}\sum_k e^{s_k} v_k$ over the keys seen so far. When the kernel does move the reference, it multiplies $l$ and $O$ by the same factor, so the two always share one $e^{-\tilde m}$, and it cancels in $O/l$; the saved log-sum-exp is $\tilde m + \log l$ for the same reason. The true max was never needed for correctness. The threshold only bounds how big an unnormalized weight can get: if the reference lags the true max by at most $\tau$ (in log2 units, as the code measures it), every weight is at most $2^{\tau}$.

blocks.tex: \frac{O}{l} = \frac{e^{-\tilde m}\sum_k e^{s_k} v_k}{e^{-\tilde m}\sum_k e^{s_k}} = \frac{\sum_k e^{s_k} v_k}{\sum_k e^{s_k}}
blocks.caption: Any common reference $\tilde m$ cancels. The max matters only for range: it keeps $e^{s - \tilde m}$ from overflowing the type that $P$ is stored in.

blocks.prompt: Rerun the lesson 1 example with this rule. Block 2 raises the max from 3 to 5, a jump of $2 \log_2 e = 2.885$ in log2 units. Does FlashAttention-4 rescale, and is the final answer still 42.347?
blocks.reveal: **No rescale, same answer.** $2.885 < 8$, so the kernel keeps $m = 3$. Block 2's weights become $e^{2-3} = 0.3679$ and $e^{5-3} = 7.389$ (bigger than 1, which is fine), block 3's are 0.0821 and 2.7183. Then $l = 11.6926$ and $O = 495.15$, and $O/l = 42.347$, exactly as before. Zero rescale operations instead of one.

blocks.title: Lesson 1 example with conditional rescaling (tau = 8)

scenes.caption: Block 1 is identical to plain online softmax: $m = 3$, $l = 1.1353$, $O = 21.353$.
Block 2's max is 5, a jump of 2.885 log2 units, below 8. No rescale: weights are taken against $m = 3$, so the 5 gives $e^{2} = 7.389$. $l = 8.8923$, $O = 327.95$.
Block 3 adds 0.0821 and 2.7183: $l = 11.693$, $O = 495.15$. Dividing gives 42.347, the exact answer. Values up to $2^8$ larger than usual are why $\tau$ must keep $P$ inside the input type's range.

blocks.md: Misconception: "the final division by $l$ fixes any scaling." It cancels a factor shared by $O$ and $l$, but not a weight that was clipped when $P$ was cast to a 16-bit or 8-bit type before $PV$. That is why $\tau$ is bounded by the type's range.

The code makes that range budget explicit. $P$ is cast to the input type before $PV$, and in log2 units the largest value of each type is about 16.0 for FP16 ($\log_2 65504$), 128 for BF16 and 8.81 for FP8 e4m3 ($\log_2 448$). The FP8 path also multiplies $P$ by $2^8$ (an offset of 8): $P$ lies in $(0, 1]$, which would leave FP8's values above 1 unused, so the offset spends them on small probabilities instead. The rule the code asserts is offset $+\ \tau <$ log2 of the type's max. FP16 uses offset 0 and $\tau = 8$ ($8 < 16.0$); FP8 uses offset 8 and $\tau = 0$ ($8 < 8.81$). A source comment says what goes wrong past the limit: the top probabilities saturate at the type's max while the FP32 denominator still counts them in full, which shrinks the output.

blocks.question: Why does FlashAttention-4 emulate only 10 to 25% of exponentials in software instead of all of them?
options: The polynomial is too inaccurate for more than a quarter of the row
Emulation uses extra registers, register bandwidth and latency; doing all of them would cause spills and leave MUFU idle
FMA units can only process one row in four
MUFU is faster than the FMA units for every input
blocks.explain: The goal is to split the work between two units that can run in parallel. The paper says full emulation would raise register pressure and could cause spills that cancel the gain, so the fraction is tuned to the MMA-to-exp ratio of each tile shape. Accuracy is not the limit: after BF16 rounding the polynomial matches hardware.

blocks.question: You add an FP8 path to a FlashAttention-4-style kernel. It already multiplies $P$ by $2^8$ before casting to e4m3 (largest value 448). Which rescale threshold $\tau$, in log2 units, is safe?
options: Any $\tau$, because the final division by $l$ corrects everything
$\tau = 8$, the same as for FP16
$\tau = 0$: the offset already uses 8 of the 8.81 log2 units FP8 has
$\tau = 16$, since FP8 needs larger weights to avoid underflow
blocks.explain: Weights can reach $2^{\text{offset} + \tau}$ before the cast. With offset 8, any $\tau \ge 0.81$ lets the largest probabilities exceed 448 and saturate, while the FP32 sum $l$ still counts them in full, so the output shrinks. The division by $l$ cannot undo a value that was clipped before $PV$. FP16, with offset 0 and a max near $2^{16}$, has room for $\tau = 8$.

blocks.md: The backward pass receives $dO$, the gradient of the loss with respect to the output; here a $d$ in front of a matrix name means a gradient, not the head dimension. It runs five MMAs per tile: recompute $S = QK^\top$, then $dP = dO\,V^\top$, $dV = P^\top dO$, $dK = dS^\top Q$ and $dQ = dS\,K$. These follow from the chain rule for a matrix product: for $O = PV$ it gives $dP = dO\,V^\top$ and $dV = P^\top dO$, and the same rule for $S = QK^\top$ gives $dQ$ and $dK$ (the $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale is left out here). In between, $dS$ comes from $P$ and $dP$ elementwise through the softmax's derivative: $dS_{ij}$ is $P_{ij}$ times the difference $dP_{ij} - D_i$, where $D_i = \sum_j P_{ij}\, dP_{ij} = dO_i \cdot O_i$ is precomputed for every row before the main loop (derived in lesson 2).

As in lesson 2, each thread block owns a K/V tile and loops over query tiles, so $dK$ and $dV$ accumulate on chip while every K/V tile adds its piece of $dQ$ into HBM with atomic adds. Those atomic adds are what FlashAttention-4 works to cut, and what its deterministic mode has to tame.

With $M = N = d = 128$ the paper's roofline gives 2560 cycles of MMA, 1024 of exponential, and 3328 of shared memory traffic: 2048 for MMA operands, 256 to write $dS$, and 1024 to write $dQ$ in FP32 and read it back for the reduction. The arithmetic: five matmuls of $2 \cdot 128^3$ FLOPs at 8192 per cycle are $5 \times 512 = 2560$ cycles; recomputing $P$ is $128^2/16 = 1024$ cycles of exponentials; the MMAs read eight $128 \times 128$ BF16 operand tiles from shared memory at 256 cycles each, 2048; $dS$ is $128^2 \times 2$ bytes over 128 bytes per cycle, 256; and $dQ$ in FP32 is 65,536 bytes, 512 cycles to write and 512 to read. Shared memory, not math, is the limit, by 30%.

blocks.title: B200 backward roofline per tile (cycles)

scenes.caption: 1-CTA, $M = N = d = 128$: SMEM total 3328 vs 2560 for the tensor cores ($3328/2560 = 1.3$).
2-CTA mode ($M = 256$ split over a CTA pair): operand traffic falls to 1536 and dQ traffic to 512, at the cost of 384 cycles of distributed shared memory exchange. Total 2688, only 5% above MMA.

blocks.md: Two ideas get there. First, **TMEM**: FlashAttention-3 held accumulators in registers, which forced an almost serial order (S, dP, dV, dQ, dK). FlashAttention-4 keeps intermediates in TMEM, recomputes the tiles transposed ($S^\top$, $P^\top$) so they sit in TMEM in exactly the operand layout the dV and dK MMAs read, and overlaps the dK and dQ MMAs of the previous tile with the softmax work of the current one. TMEM cannot hold five accumulators, so S and P share one region and dP, dS and dQ share another.

Second, **2-CTA MMA**: with tile $M = 256$, each CTA of the pair stages only half of operand B in its own SMEM. The dQ MMA reduces over the key dimension, which the pair has split, so the CTAs swap halves of $dS$ through distributed shared memory (DSMEM). Each CTA then owns $M/2$ rows with the full $2N$ reduction and writes only half of the dQ tile, which also halves the number of global atomic adds.

blocks.title: 2-CTA backward dQ step (simplified)

scenes.caption: Each CTA stages only half of operand B; the paired MMA reads both halves. That is where the operand traffic drop from 2048 to 1536 cycles comes from.
For dQ the reduction axis is split across the pair, so the CTAs exchange halves of $dS$ over DSMEM. That costs 384 cycles in the roofline, much less than it saves.
Each CTA now writes only its half of the dQ tile, so the pair issues half as many global atomic adds as two independent CTAs would.

blocks.md: Atomic adds make dQ (and dK, dV with grouped-query attention, where several query heads share one K/V head so its gradients are summed across thread blocks) nondeterministic: floating point addition is not associative (adding a and b first, then c, can give different last bits than adding b and c first, then a), and the order of atomic adds changes run to run. FlashAttention-4 offers a **deterministic mode** that serializes the reductions with a semaphore (a counter in memory that each thread block waits on until it is its turn) in a fixed order, using CTA swizzling (remapping which tile each CTA works on) and a shortest-processing-time-first order for causal masks to limit stalls. The paper reports up to 75% of the nondeterministic 1-CTA speed; the later blog post reports 85 to 90%.

**Scheduling.** With causal masking, query tiles near the start of the sequence have short loops and tiles near the end have long ones. Launched in the natural order, SMs pick up the short tiles first and the long ones last, leaving a ragged tail. FlashAttention-4 uses **longest-processing-time-first (LPT)** ordering, swizzling heads into sections that fit in L2 cache (reordering work so the heads processed together stay in the L2, the on-chip cache all SMs share). It works on any GPU: the authors measured 4 to 8% gains for MHA (multi-head attention), where every query head has its own K and V, and 7 to 14% for MQA (multi-query attention), where all query heads share one K and V head, on an H200 (an H100 with larger, faster HBM) with FlashAttention-3.

For variable-length batches, a preprocessing kernel sorts batches by cost. Such batches pack sequences of different lengths together; in inference they mix prefills, which process a whole prompt at once, and decodes, which generate one new token per step against a cached context that can be very long.

blocks.title: Toy causal workload: 4 tiles of length 1 to 4 on 2 SMs

scenes.caption: Natural order (shortest first), each tile going to the first free SM: the longest tile starts last and the job ends at 6 units, with SM 1 idle for the last 2.
Longest first: SM 1 takes 4 then 1, SM 2 takes 3 then 2, and both finish at 5. Same work, about 17% less wall time, with no change to the kernel's math.

blocks.question: What is the main reason FlashAttention-4 uses the 2-CTA MMA mode in the backward pass?
options: To double the tensor core FLOPs available to each CTA
To cut shared memory traffic (each CTA stages half of operand B) and halve dQ atomic adds
To make the backward pass deterministic
To fit five accumulators in tensor memory
blocks.explain: The backward pass is limited by shared memory bandwidth (3328 vs 2560 cycles). Pairing CTAs means each stages half of B, and the dS exchange lets each CTA own half of the dQ tile, halving atomics. Peak FLOPs are unchanged, and determinism comes from the separate semaphore mode.

blocks.question: A varlen inference batch contains short prefills followed by a few very long-context decodes. Which FlashAttention-4 scheduling idea addresses the resulting slowdown?
options: Conditional softmax rescaling
Sorting batches by their per-tile cost so the longest work starts first (LPT)
Emulating the exponential on FMA units
Switching to FP8
blocks.explain: This is load imbalance: if long work is processed last, a few SMs finish late while others sit idle. The paper launches a small preprocessing kernel to sort batches by cost and write a virtual-to-actual batch index map, which can be cached so sorting costs nothing on later calls.

lessons.title: Using and measuring the kernels: benchmarks, numerics, decoding

blocks.md: Everything so far was about one kernel's internals. This lesson is about using it: calling it, timing it, checking its accuracy, and reshaping it for decoding. Start with the shape most inference engineers meet first, a decode step: batch 1, 16 heads, one new query row per head and a 32K-token KV cache. The forward grid has one thread block per (batch, head, query tile), so it launches 16 thread blocks on a GPU with 132 SMs, and each walks all 32K keys alone. Most of the GPU idles. The fix comes at the end of the lesson, after measurement and numerics.

**Implementation and results.** FlashAttention-4 is written entirely in CuTe-DSL, the Python-embedded domain-specific language of CUTLASS, which compiles to PTX, NVIDIA's assembly-like virtual instruction set, and then to machine code. Compiling one kernel took 2.5 s for the forward and 1.4 s for the backward, versus 55 s and 45 s for FlashAttention-3's C++ templates (22x and 32x faster). On B200 with BF16 the paper reports up to 1613 TFLOPs/s, 71.7% of 2.25 PFLOPS, 1.1 to 1.3x faster than cuDNN 9.13 and 2.1 to 2.7x faster than Triton (OpenAI's Python-based language and compiler for GPU kernels) in the forward pass. The authors note that newer cuDNN releases have since adopted many of these techniques and perform similarly.

# FlashAttention-3 (Hopper): built from the repo's hopper/ directory
from flash_attn_3 import flash_attn_interface
out = flash_attn_interface.flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True)

# FlashAttention-4 (CuTe-DSL, Hopper and Blackwell): pip install flash-attn-4

out, lse = flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True)  # lse is None unless return_lse=True or grads are needed

blocks.md: **Measuring.** Benchmarks report TFLOPs/s from lesson 3's formula: $4 \cdot N^2 \cdot d \cdot \text{heads} \cdot \text{batch}$ FLOPs over the measured time, halved for causal and multiplied by 2.5 for the backward. Utilization is that divided by the GPU's dense peak (989 TFLOPS for H100 FP16). The FlashAttention-3 paper's setup is a good template: an H100 80GB SXM5 with the clock fixed at 1830 MHz (the clock the 989 assumes), sequence lengths 512 to 16k with the batch chosen so every run has 16k tokens, hidden dimension 2048 (16 heads at $d = 128$), and the average of 100 repetitions. The *Microbenchmarking pitfalls* course covers warm-up, clocks and statistics in general.

scenes.caption: FlashAttention-3, non-causal, from the FA3 paper's benchmark figure: 467 to 648 TFLOPs/s, 47% to 65.5% of the 989 peak. Each run has 16k tokens.
FlashAttention-2 on the same GPU and shapes: 309 to 370 TFLOPs/s, 31% to 37%. It flattens early: the synchronous design, not the sequence length, is its ceiling.
